paras: The lynching of Billy Cole was the hanging of William "Billy" Cole, accused of shooting two men at a dance, by twelve masked men who took him from the lockup at Guide Rock, Nebraska, early on August 20, 1888. He was hanged from a railroad bridge while both men he had wounded were reported alive, and the lynchers were not identified. Wire reports carried the story nationally the next day, and some Nebraska editors treated it lightly.

According to an Omaha Bee special dated August 18, Cole, a young man "who desires the reputation of a western desperado," had been ejected for drunkenness from a dance at Talbot's hall the night before. When the dance broke up he fired four shots into the departing crowd, hitting Billy Montgomery in the right hip and Charley Grant, a clerk in the Guide Rock bank, in the right side above the stomach. Fifty to one hundred townspeople hunted him through the night and captured him the next morning, and the Bee's correspondent reported "strong talk of lynching him" if Grant died.

Other dispatches said he had the revolver from a companion named Henderson, or that he fired because women would not dance with him. The St. Paul Globe called Cole "a very hard character" who had left Texas after a shooting and claimed kinship with the Younger outlaws.

The Globe's Guide Rock correspondent wrote that an attempt by Cole's lawyer to have him moved on a writ of habeas corpus to the insecure county jail at Red Cloud "precipitated matters." The Bee's special said instead that friends of the wounded men had "sworn vengeance" and waited for the guards to relax their vigilance.

At about 2 a.m. on August 20, twelve masked men surrounded the lockup, overpowered the two guards at revolver point, broke the outside door with a sledge hammer, and took Cole and the guards to the railroad bridge just east of town. With a rope around his neck, Cole admitted the shooting, saying he had no malice toward the men he shot and had been drunk. Ordered to jump, he refused and was pushed off; he fell about eight feet, his neck was broken, and he died almost at once.

The coroner at Cowles was notified and held an inquest, but no report of its findings appears in the coverage. The Globe wrote that the lynchers were unknown and that "no attempt will be made to ascertain" who they were; no report of arrests was found. According to the Bee special, "the best citizens" of Guide Rock regretted the lynching but blamed recent escapes from the Red Cloud jail; Grant was reported in precarious condition but likely to live.

On August 21 a wire version of the Bee special ran from New York to Savannah, where the Morning News headlined it "Lynchers in a Hurry." The St. Paul Globe ran its own special as "Lynched a Bad Man." Weekly digests cut the story to a line, sometimes placing Guide Rock in Arkansas or "near Omaha," while the full Bee special was reprinted into September as "Bold Nebraska Vigilantes" and "Hung by Twelve Masked Men."

The papers called Cole a "desperado," a "bad man," a "hard case" and a "young tough," and none stated his race. Some Nebraska editors treated the hanging lightly: the Beatrice Daily Express called Cole "the latest acquisition to the rather liberal crop of railroad bridge fruit this year," and the O'Neill Frontier added that it was "now Iowa's turn." The Omaha Bee passed along the Hastings Gazette-Journal's remark that Cole was lynched "before his executioners knew that his victim would die." The Bee's year-end review paired it with the Pawnee City lynching of Fremont Emmons, calling Cole "a desperado who killed two men at a dance."

The Beatrice Daily Express said Grant had died an hour or two before the lynching and the Frontier called Cole his murderer, but the wire report and both Guide Rock specials, the nearest reports, said both men were alive. The Bee's December statement that Cole "killed two men" conflicts with all the August reports from Guide Rock, and the Midland Journal alone said his companion Henderson was taken to the bridge with him.

reader.title: Lynching of Billy Cole
bases: Twelve masked men took Cole from the lockup at Guide Rock and hanged him from a railroad bridge (A8, A9, A34).

Twelve masked men overpowered the guards, took Cole from custody and hanged him without trial (A8, A9, A34); they acted on the accusation that he shot two men, after talk of lynching if a victim died (A1, A34).
The St. Paul Globe special (A8, A9), the Omaha Bee special (A34, A7) and the wire report (A4) independently agree on the core event.

accounts.gist: Lynchers had meant to await Grant's fate, but a habeas corpus move to transfer Cole to the insecure Red Cloud jail precipitated the hanging; lynchers unknown and not to be sought.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee Guide Rock special
accounts.gist: Friends of the wounded men had sworn vengeance and waited for the guards to relax; a coroner held an inquest; local citizens regretted the lynching but blamed jail escapes at Red Cloud.

framing.detail: Wire and digest items ('A Meb Lynchen Billy Cole', 'Lynchers in a Hurry') reported it flatly, often noting both victims were alive.
The Globe ('Lynched a Bad Man') and Bee specials stressed Cole's bad record; the Bee special relayed local regret while blaming the Red Cloud jail.
The Beatrice Daily Express ('railroad bridge fruit') and the Frontier ('It is now Iowa's turn') treated the hanging with levity.
The Hastings Gazette-Journal, quoted by the Bee, called it 'the little affair' and noted he was lynched before his victim was known to die.
